name: Elizabeth Moos
bio: Elizabeth Moos was an educator and a co-defendant of W. E. B. Du Bois in the 1951 prosecution of the officers of the Peace Information Center, which had circulated the Stockholm peace appeal against nuclear weapons. Indicted in February 1951 for failing to register as agents of a foreign principal, she was handcuffed and booked; the defendants were acquitted when the trial finally collapsed in November 1951.
charges: Failure to register as the agent of a foreign principal under the Foreign Agents Registration Act, as an officer of the Peace Information Center — a prosecution for peace advocacy.
convicted: No — the case ended in acquittal/dismissal in November 1951 after the government failed to prove the Center was a foreign agent.

name: Kyrle Elkin
bio: Kyrle Elkin was a co-defendant of W. E. B. Du Bois in the 1951 Foreign Agents Registration Act prosecution of the Peace Information Center, charged for the Center's campaign against the atomic bomb. The defendants were acquitted when the case collapsed in November 1951.
charges: Failure to register as a foreign agent under FARA, as an officer of the Peace Information Center.
convicted: No — acquitted/dismissed, November 1951.

name: Abbott Simon
bio: Abbott Simon was a co-defendant of W. E. B. Du Bois in the 1951 prosecution of the Peace Information Center under the Foreign Agents Registration Act, brought over the Center's anti-nuclear peace campaign. The case ended in acquittal in November 1951.
charges: Failure to register as a foreign agent under FARA, as an officer of the Peace Information Center.
convicted: No — acquitted/dismissed, November 1951.

name: Sylvia Soloff
bio: Sylvia Soloff, a clerical worker for the Peace Information Center, was indicted in 1951 with W. E. B. Du Bois and the Center's other officers for failing to register as foreign agents — a prosecution over the Center's anti-atomic-bomb peace appeal. The case ended in acquittal in November 1951.
charges: Failure to register as a foreign agent under FARA, as a worker for the Peace Information Center.
convicted: No — acquitted/dismissed, November 1951.

name: Julius Emspak
bio: Julius Emspak was the secretary-treasurer of the United Electrical, Radio and Machine Workers (UE), one of the most militant left-led unions of the era. Cited for contempt of Congress after refusing, on First and Fifth Amendment grounds, to answer the House Un-American Activities Committee's questions about Communist affiliation, he was convicted in 1951 and sentenced to six months in jail and a $500 fine; his conviction was eventually overturned by the Supreme Court (Emspak v. United States, 1955).
charges: Contempt of Congress — for refusing to answer HUAC's questions about Communist affiliation.
convicted: Convicted in 1951 (six months and a $500 fine); the conviction was later reversed by the U.S. Supreme Court.
sentence: Six months in jail and a $500 fine (later overturned on appeal).

name: James Matles
bio: James Matles was the director of organization of the United Electrical Workers (UE) and one of its founders. Prosecuted for contempt of Congress for refusing to answer HUAC's questions about Communist ties, he was acquitted in 1951; he was later the target of a long government effort to strip his citizenship.
charges: Contempt of Congress — for refusing to answer HUAC's questions about Communist affiliation.
convicted: No — acquitted in 1951.

name: Tom Quinn
bio: Tom Quinn was an officer of UE Local 601 in Pittsburgh who was prosecuted for contempt of Congress after refusing to answer the House Un-American Activities Committee. He was fined and given a jail term in 1951, which he appealed, in one of a wave of contempt cases against UE leaders who would not name names.
charges: Contempt of Congress — for refusing to answer HUAC's questions (UE Local 601, Pittsburgh).
convicted: Convicted of contempt in 1951; appealed.

name: Thomas Fitzpatrick
bio: Thomas J. Fitzpatrick, a leader of UE Local 601 in Pittsburgh, was tried for contempt of Congress for refusing to answer HUAC's questions about Communist affiliation. He was acquitted in 1951.
charges: Contempt of Congress — for refusing to answer HUAC (UE Local 601, Pittsburgh).
convicted: No — acquitted in 1951.

name: Talmadge Raley
bio: Talmadge Raley, a UE leader from Cincinnati, was prosecuted for contempt of Congress for refusing to answer HUAC's questions about Communism. He was acquitted in 1951.
charges: Contempt of Congress — for refusing to answer HUAC (UE, Cincinnati).
convicted: No — acquitted in 1951.

name: Esther Vice
bio: Esther Vice was a Cincinnati leader of the United Electrical Workers prosecuted for contempt of Congress after declining to answer the House Un-American Activities Committee. She was acquitted in 1951.
charges: Contempt of Congress — for refusing to answer HUAC (UE, Cincinnati).
convicted: No — acquitted in 1951.

name: Frank Panzino
bio: Frank Panzino, a Pittsburgh UE unionist, was prosecuted for contempt of Congress for refusing to answer HUAC's questions about Communist affiliation. He was acquitted in 1951.
charges: Contempt of Congress — for refusing to answer HUAC (UE, Pittsburgh).
convicted: No — acquitted in 1951.

name: Frederick Vanderbilt Field
bio: Frederick Vanderbilt Field, a wealthy heir who broke with his class to become a radical, was a trustee of the Civil Rights Congress Bail Fund. When a federal grand jury demanded the names of the fund's contributors after four Smith Act Communists jumped bail, Field refused and was jailed for contempt in 1951, serving some nine months.
charges: Contempt of court — for refusing to surrender the contributor list of the Civil Rights Congress Bail Fund.
convicted: Convicted of contempt and jailed in 1951.

name: Dashiell Hammett
bio: Dashiell Hammett — the celebrated author of The Maltese Falcon and a veteran of both World Wars — was a trustee of the Civil Rights Congress Bail Fund. In 1951 he refused to tell a federal court who had contributed to the fund and was jailed for about six months for contempt; he was blacklisted and pursued for back taxes for the rest of his life.
charges: Contempt of court — for refusing to name contributors to the Civil Rights Congress Bail Fund.
convicted: Convicted of contempt and jailed in 1951.

name: Alphaeus Hunton
bio: Dr. W. Alphaeus Hunton was a Black scholar and anti-colonial activist, a leader of the Council on African Affairs, and a trustee of the Civil Rights Congress Bail Fund. In 1951 he was jailed for about six months for contempt after refusing to give a federal court the names of the fund's contributors.
charges: Contempt of court — for refusing to name contributors to the Civil Rights Congress Bail Fund.
convicted: Convicted of contempt and jailed in 1951.

name: Abner Green
affiliation: American Committee for Protection of Foreign Born
bio: Abner Green was the executive secretary of the American Committee for Protection of Foreign Born and a trustee of the Civil Rights Congress Bail Fund. He was jailed for contempt in 1951 for refusing to reveal the fund's contributors, and spent much of the 1950s fighting deportation and contempt prosecutions.
charges: Contempt of court — for refusing to name contributors to the Civil Rights Congress Bail Fund.
convicted: Convicted of contempt and jailed in 1951.

name: George Crockett
bio: George W. Crockett Jr. was one of the defense attorneys in the 1949 Foley Square Smith Act trial of the eleven Communist Party leaders. Like his co-counsel, he was summarily sentenced to prison for contempt of court by Judge Harold Medina for his vigorous defense; he served four months in 1951. Crockett went on to become a Detroit judge and a member of Congress.
charges: Contempt of court — for his conduct defending the eleven Communist Party leaders at the Foley Square Smith Act trial.
convicted: Convicted of contempt; sentenced to four months, served in 1951.

name: Harry Sacher
bio: Harry Sacher was a defense attorney at the 1949 Foley Square trial of the eleven Communist Party leaders. For his courtroom defense, Judge Harold Medina found him in contempt and sentenced him to prison; the Supreme Court upheld the contempt convictions of the lawyers in 1952 (Sacher v. United States), and he was also subjected to disbarment proceedings.
charges: Contempt of court — for defending the eleven Communist leaders at the Foley Square Smith Act trial.
convicted: Convicted of contempt (upheld in Sacher v. United States, 1952); jailed and faced disbarment.

name: Abraham Isserman
bio: Abraham J. Isserman was a defense lawyer at the 1949 Foley Square Smith Act trial of the eleven Communist Party leaders. Cited for contempt by Judge Medina, he was jailed and disbarred for his defense of the case — among the harshest reprisals against any of the lawyers.
charges: Contempt of court — for defending the eleven Communist leaders at the Foley Square trial.
convicted: Convicted of contempt; jailed and disbarred.
sentence: Several months in prison, plus disbarment.

name: Helen Bryan
bio: Helen R. Bryan was the executive secretary of the Joint Anti-Fascist Refugee Committee, which aided refugees from Franco's Spain. Convicted of contempt of Congress for refusing to surrender the committee's records to HUAC, she served a three-month sentence at the federal women's reformatory at Alderson in 1950–51.
charges: Contempt of Congress — for refusing to give HUAC the records of the Joint Anti-Fascist Refugee Committee.
convicted: Convicted of contempt of Congress.
sentence: Three months at the Alderson federal reformatory.

name: Ernestina Fleischman
bio: Ernestina Fleischman was an official of the Joint Anti-Fascist Refugee Committee jailed for contempt of Congress after refusing to turn over the committee's records to the House Un-American Activities Committee; she served three months at Alderson alongside Helen Bryan.
charges: Contempt of Congress — for refusing to surrender the Joint Anti-Fascist Refugee Committee's records.
convicted: Convicted of contempt of Congress.
sentence: Three months at the Alderson federal reformatory.

name: Dorothy Healey
bio: Dorothy Ray Healey was the best-known Communist organizer in Southern California, a veteran of the 1930s farm-labor strikes. She was among the fifteen California Communist leaders arrested in July 1951 under the Smith Act and held on heavy bail; convicted in 1952, she won reversal under the Supreme Court's 1957 Yates decision.
charges: Smith Act — conspiring to advocate the overthrow of the government, as a California Communist Party leader.
convicted: Arrested July 1951; convicted 1952; conviction set aside after Yates v. United States (1957).
sentence: Five years and a fine; reversed on appeal.

name: Rose Chernin
bio: Rose Chernin was a Los Angeles Communist organizer and a leader of the Los Angeles Committee for Protection of the Foreign Born. Arrested in the July 1951 Smith Act roundup of California Communist leaders and held on $50,000 bail, she was convicted in 1952; the conviction was overturned after Yates v. United States.
charges: Smith Act — conspiring to advocate the overthrow of the government (California CP leader).
convicted: Arrested 1951; convicted 1952; reversed after Yates (1957).

name: Philip Connelly
bio: Philip 'Slim' Connelly was a California labor journalist and former head of the Los Angeles CIO Council, and editor of the Daily People's World. He was among the California Smith Act defendants arrested in 1951 and held on heavy bail.
charges: Smith Act — conspiring to advocate the overthrow of the government (California CP/labor leader).
convicted: Arrested 1951; tried with the California Smith Act group.

name: Harry Steinberg
bio: Harry Steinberg was one of the fifteen California Communist Party leaders arrested in Los Angeles in July 1951 under the Smith Act and held on $75,000 bail pending trial.
charges: Smith Act — conspiring to advocate the overthrow of the government (California CP leader).
convicted: Arrested 1951; tried with the California Smith Act group.

name: Al Richmond
bio: Al Richmond was the editor of the San Francisco Daily People's World, the West Coast Communist newspaper. He was among the California Smith Act defendants arrested in 1951 and held on $75,000 bail — one of several Communist editors jailed in the roundup.
charges: Smith Act — conspiring to advocate the overthrow of the government (newspaper editor / CP leader).
convicted: Arrested 1951; convicted; reversed after Yates (1957).

name: Ernest Fox
bio: Ernest Fox was one of the Northern California Communist Party leaders arrested in San Francisco in July 1951 under the Smith Act and held on heavy bail.
charges: Smith Act — conspiring to advocate the overthrow of the government (California CP leader).
convicted: Arrested 1951; tried with the California Smith Act group.

name: Carl Lambert
bio: Carl Lambert was among the California Communist Party leaders arrested in 1951 under the Smith Act and held on $75,000 bail in the San Francisco group of defendants.
charges: Smith Act — conspiring to advocate the overthrow of the government (California CP leader).
convicted: Arrested 1951; tried with the California Smith Act group.

name: Albert Lima
bio: Albert 'Mickey' Lima was a Northern California Communist Party leader arrested in San Francisco in the July 1951 Smith Act roundup and held on heavy bail.
charges: Smith Act — conspiring to advocate the overthrow of the government (California CP leader).
convicted: Arrested 1951; convicted; reversed after Yates (1957).

name: Oleta O'Connor Yates
bio: Oleta O'Connor Yates was the organizational secretary of the California Communist Party and the lead named defendant in the state's Smith Act case. Arrested in 1951 and jailed in Los Angeles, her appeal produced the landmark 1957 Supreme Court decision Yates v. United States, which gutted Smith Act prosecutions nationwide.
charges: Smith Act — conspiring to advocate the overthrow of the government (lead California CP defendant).
convicted: Arrested 1951; convicted 1952; conviction reversed in Yates v. United States (1957).
sentence: Five years; reversed by the Supreme Court.

name: Loretta Stack
bio: Loretta Starvus Stack was among the California Communist Party leaders indicted under the Smith Act in 1951 and a defendant in the case that became Yates v. United States.
charges: Smith Act — conspiring to advocate the overthrow of the government (California CP leader).
convicted: Arrested 1951; convicted; reversed after Yates (1957).

name: Bernadette Doyle
bio: Bernadette Doyle was a California Communist Party leader — a perennial candidate who had once polled 600,000 votes statewide — arrested in the 1951 Smith Act roundup and held on low bail relative to her co-defendants.
charges: Smith Act — conspiring to advocate the overthrow of the government (California CP leader).
convicted: Arrested 1951; tried with the California Smith Act group.

name: William Schneiderman
bio: William Schneiderman was the secretary of the California Communist Party and, after the 1951 arrests, its acting national head. Seized in New York on $100,000 bail and taken to California in handcuffs, he was a lead Smith Act defendant; he had earlier been the subject of the Supreme Court's 1943 Schneiderman v. United States denaturalization case.
charges: Smith Act — conspiring to advocate the overthrow of the government (California CP secretary).
convicted: Arrested 1951; convicted 1952; reversed after Yates (1957).

name: Maurice Braverman
bio: Maurice Braverman was a Baltimore attorney prosecuted as one of the six Maryland Smith Act defendants in 1951 — though not himself charged as a Communist Party member, but for his association as a movement lawyer. He was convicted and disbarred, and served time before resuming his legal career.
charges: Smith Act — conspiring to advocate the overthrow of the government (Baltimore defendants).
convicted: Arrested 1951; convicted; later disbarred and imprisoned.
sentence: Three years; reversed/remitted after later Smith Act rulings.

name: Dorothy Rose Blumberg
bio: Dorothy Rose Blumberg was one of the six Maryland Communist Party leaders arrested under the Smith Act in 1951; arrested in New York and returned to Baltimore, she could not raise the $20,000 bail.
charges: Smith Act — conspiring to advocate the overthrow of the government (Baltimore CP leader).
convicted: Arrested 1951; convicted with the Baltimore group.

name: Phil Frankfeld
bio: Philip Frankfeld was the chairman of the Maryland-District of Columbia Communist Party and the lead of the six Baltimore Smith Act defendants arrested in 1951.
charges: Smith Act — conspiring to advocate the overthrow of the government (Baltimore CP chairman).
convicted: Arrested 1951; convicted with the Baltimore group.

name: Andrew Onda
bio: Andrew Onda was a western Pennsylvania Communist Party leader prosecuted under both the Pennsylvania state sedition law and the federal Smith Act in 1951, arrested in the FBI's Pittsburgh roundup while a state sedition trial was still underway.
charges: Pennsylvania sedition law and the Smith Act — as a Pittsburgh Communist Party leader.
convicted: Convicted under the state sedition law (1951); also a federal Smith Act defendant.
sentence: State sedition conviction (later voided after Pennsylvania v. Nelson, 1956).

name: James Dolsen
bio: James Dolsen was an elderly Pittsburgh Communist and journalist tried under the Pennsylvania sedition law and indicted under the federal Smith Act in 1951.
charges: Pennsylvania sedition law and the Smith Act — as a Pittsburgh Communist Party leader.
convicted: Convicted under the state sedition law (1951); federal Smith Act defendant.
sentence: State sedition conviction (later voided after Pennsylvania v. Nelson).

name: William Albertson
bio: William Albertson was a Communist Party leader arrested in Michigan in 1951 for removal to Pittsburgh as one of the western Pennsylvania Smith Act defendants. (He was later, in 1964, expelled from the Party after the FBI forged a document to frame him as an informer.)
charges: Smith Act — conspiring to advocate the overthrow of the government (Pittsburgh group).
convicted: Arrested 1951; tried with the Pittsburgh Smith Act defendants.

name: Jack Hall
bio: Jack Hall was the regional director of the International Longshore and Warehouse Union (ILWU) in Hawaii, where the union had transformed the islands' plantation economy. His arrest in August 1951 was the first Smith Act arrest of a ranking union leader; convicted in 1953, he won reversal after the Yates decision.
charges: Smith Act — conspiring to advocate the overthrow of the government, as ILWU regional director (the 'Hawaii Seven').
convicted: Arrested August 1951; convicted 1953; conviction reversed in 1958 after Yates.

name: Charles Fujimoto
bio: Charles Fujimoto was the chairman of the Communist Party of Hawaii and a lead defendant among the 'Hawaii Seven' arrested under the Smith Act in August 1951.
charges: Smith Act — conspiring to advocate the overthrow of the government (chairman, CP of Hawaii).
convicted: Arrested August 1951; convicted 1953; reversed after Yates (1958).

name: Koji Ariyoshi
bio: Koji Ariyoshi was the editor of the Honolulu Record, a progressive labor weekly, and a World War II veteran who had served with the U.S. mission to the Chinese Communists. He was one of the 'Hawaii Seven' arrested under the Smith Act in 1951; convicted in 1953, his conviction was reversed after Yates.
charges: Smith Act — conspiring to advocate the overthrow of the government (newspaper editor; Hawaii Seven).
convicted: Arrested August 1951; convicted 1953; reversed after Yates (1958).
